{{Short description|Key derivation function based on an HMAC}}
{{confused|Hong Kong Democratic Foundation}}

'''HKDF''' is a multi-purpose [[key derivation function]] (KDF) based on the [[HMAC]] [[message authentication code]]. HKDF follows "extract-then-expand" paradigm, where the KDF logically consists of two modules: the first stage takes the input keying material and "extracts" from it a fixed-length pseudorandom key, and then the second stage "expands" this key into several additional, independent pseudorandom keys as the output of the KDF.

==Mechanism==

HKDF is the composition of two functions, HKDF-Extract and HKDF-Expand:{{r|iacr}}{{rp|11}}

<math display="block">
\operatorname{HKDF}(\mathit{salt}, \mathit{IKM}, \mathit{info}, L)
=
\operatorname{HKDF{-}Expand}
\!\left(
\operatorname{HKDF{-}Extract}(\mathit{salt}, \mathit{IKM}),
\mathit{info},
L
\right)
</math>

===HKDF-Extract===

HKDF-Extract (<math>\mathrm{XTR}</math>) takes "input key material" or "source key material" (<math>\mathrm{IKM}</math> or <math>\mathrm{SKM}</math>) such as a [[shared secret]] generated using [[Diffie-Hellman]]; an optional, non-secret, random or [[pseudorandom]] [[salt (cryptography)|salt]] (<math>r</math>); and generates a cryptographic key called the <math>\mathrm{PRK}</math> ("pseudorandom key"). HKDF-Extract acts as a "[[randomness extractor]]",{{efn|In complexity theory, informally, an extractor maps input probability distributions with sufficient entropy into output distributions that are statistically close to uniform.{{r|iacr}}{{rp|4}}}}{{r|iacr}}{{rp|1}} specifically a "computational extractor", taking a potentially non-uniform value of sufficient [[min-entropy]] and generating a value [[Computational indistinguishability|indistinguishable]] from a uniform random value (pseudorandom).{{r|iacr}}{{rp|9–11}}{{r|uklec}} Computational extractors assume attackers are computationally bounded and source entropy may only exist in a [[Hard-core predicate|computational sense]]. Such extractors can be built using cryptographic functions under suitable assumptions, modeled as universal hash function (in the generic case) or a random oracle (in constrained scenarios like sources with weak entropy).{{r|iacr}}{{rp|1–3}}

Salt (<math>r</math>) acts as a "source-independent extractor",{{efn|A random salt enforces independence between the source distribution (of the initial key material) and the extractor itself, and between different uses of the same extractor scheme (for example, a specific instantiation of HMAC) by an application.{{r|iacr}}{{rp|25–26}}}} strengthening HKDF's security guarantees.<ref name="uklec">{{cite video |via=YouTube |last=Krawczyk |first=Hugo |year=2012 |publisher=[[Isaac Newton Institute for Mathematical Sciences]] |title=Cryptographic Extraction |time=16m |url=https://www.newton.ac.uk/seminar/2429/ |quote=Randomness extractors are algorithms that map sources of sufficient min-entropy to outputs that are statistically close to uniform. Randomness extraction has become a central and ubiquitous notion in complexity theory and theoretical computer science with innumerable applications and surprising and unifying connections to other notions. Cryptography, too, has greatly benefited from this notion. Cryptographic applications of randomness extractors range from the construction of pseudorandom generators from one-way functions to the design of cryptographic functionality from noisy and weak sources (including applications to quantum cryptography) to the more recent advances in areas such as leakage- and exposure-resilient cryptography, circular encryption, fully homomorphic encryption, etc. Randomness extractors have also found important cryptographic uses in practical applications, particularly for the construction of key derivation functions. In many of these applications, the defining property of randomness extractors, namely, statistical closeness of their output to a uniform distribution, can be relaxed and replaced with computational indistinguishability. Extractors that provide this form of relaxed guarantee are called 'computational extractors'. In this talk I will cover some recent advances in the understanding and applicability of computational extractors with particular focus on their role in building key derivation functions.}}</ref> Using a fixed public <math>r</math> is safe for multiple invocations of HKDF (on "independent" but secret {{itco|<em>IKM</em>}}s which may or may not be derived from the same source),{{r|iacr}}{{rp|4–6}}{{r|rfc}}{{rp|6}} provided <math>r</math> isn't chosen or manipulated by an attacker.{{r|rfc}}{{rp|6}} Ideally, <math>r</math> is a random string of hash function's output length. Even low quality <math>r</math> (weak entropy or shorter length) is recommended as they contribute "significantly" to the security of the <math>\mathrm{OKM}</math>.{{r|rfc}}{{rp|4–5}} Without or with a low-entropy, non-secret <math>r</math>, if an attacker can influence the {{itco|<math>\mathrm{IKM}</math>}}s source in a way that specifically exploits HKDF-Extract's underlying hash function (finding a collision or a specific bias), <math>\mathrm{XTR}</math> provides no protection. A random <math>r</math>, even if fixed by the application (for example, random number generators using <math>r</math> as seed), would strengthen protections for that specific extractor session.{{r|iacr}}{{rp|9,24–26}} In such a setting, sufficiently long {{itco|<math>\mathrm{IKM}</math>}}s also provide better entropy extraction.{{r|iacr}}{{rp|24}} However, allowing the attacker to influence enough of the {{itco|<math>\mathrm{IKM}</math>}} after seeing <math>r</math> may result in a completely insecure KDF.{{r|iacr}}{{rp|8–9}}

HKDF-Extract is the result of HMAC with <math>r</math> as the key (all zeros up to length of the underlying extractor hash function, if not provided) and the <math>\mathrm{IKM}</math> as the message.{{r|rfc}}{{rp|3}} The underlying hash function used for HKDF-Extract step may be different to the one used by HKDF-Expand. It is recommended that HKDF-Extract uses [[Security_level|strongest]] hash function available to the application,{{r|iacr}}{{rp|27}} as it "concentrates" the entropy already present in <math>\mathrm{IKM}</math> but may not necessarily "add" to it.{{r|rfc}}{{rp|2}} Truncated output from a stronger underlying hash function for <math>\mathrm{XTR}</math> (for example, SHA512/256) offers stronger extraction properties.{{r|iacr}}{{rp|17}} The attacker is assumed to have partial knowledge about <math>\mathrm{IKM}</math> (publicly known values in the case of Diffie-Hellman) or partial control over it (entropy pools).{{r|rfc}}{{rp|2}}

HKDF-Extract may be skipped if the <math>\mathrm{IKM}</math> is itself a cryptographically strong key (and hence can assume the role of <math>\mathrm{PRK}</math>), though it is recommended that HKDF-Extract be applied for the sake of compatibility with the general case,{{r|rfc}}{{rp|5}} especially if <math>r</math> is available to the application.

===HKDF-Expand===

HKDF-Expand (<math>\mathrm{PRF*}</math>) takes the <math>\mathrm{PRK}</math>{{r|iacr}}{{rp|9–11}} (or any random key-derivation key if HKDF-Extract step is skipped),{{r|rfc}}{{rp|5}} optional <math>info</math> (<math>\mathrm{CTXinfo}</math>), and a length (<math>L</math>), to generate output key material (<math>\mathrm{OKM}</math>) of length <math>L</math>.{{r|iacr}}{{rp|9–11}} Multiple <math>\mathrm{OKM}</math>s can be generated from a single <math>\mathrm{PRK}</math> by using different values for <math>\mathrm{CTXinfo}</math>, which must be "independent" of the <math>\mathrm{IKM}</math> passed in HKDF-Extract.{{r|rfc}}{{rp|5}} Even if an attacker, who knows <math>r</math> and some auxiliary information about the secret <math>\mathrm{IKM}</math>, can force the use of the same <math>\mathrm{IKM}</math> (and <math>\mathrm{PRK}</math>, by extension), in two or more HKDF-Expand contexts (represented by <math>\mathrm{CTXinfo}</math>), the <math>\mathrm{OKM}</math>s output are computationally independent (leak no useful information on each other).{{r|iacr}}{{rp|7–8}}

HKDF-Expand, acting as a variable-output-length [[pseudorandom function family|pseudorandom function]] (<math>\mathrm{PRF*}</math>) keyed on <math>\mathrm{PRK}</math>,{{r|iacr}}{{rp|15}} calls HMAC on <math>\mathrm{CTXinfo}</math> as the message (empty string, if unspecified) appended to an 8-bit counter <math>i</math> initialized to <math>1</math>.{{r|iacr}}{{rp|18}} Subsequent calls to HMAC are chained in "feedback mode" by prepending the previous HMAC output to <math>\mathrm{CTXinfo}</math> and incrementing <math>i</math>.{{r|rfc}} <math>\mathrm{OKM}</math> is a function of the output size (<math>k</math> bits) of HMAC's underlying hash function; i.e., [[SHA-256]] outputs <math>\mathrm{OKM}</math> in segments of <math>k=256</math> bits for up to a maximum length of

<math display="block">
255 \times k
\text{ bits}
=
255 \times 256
\text{ bits}
=
8160
\text{ bytes},
</math>

truncated to desired length <math>L</math>.{{r|iacr}}{{rp|11}}

HKDF-Expand may be skipped if <math>\mathrm{PRK}</math> is at least desired length <math>L</math>, though it is recommended that HKDF-Expand be applied for additional "smoothing" of the <math>\mathrm{OKM}</math>.{{r|iacr}}{{rp|27}}{{r|rfc}}{{rp|6}}

== Standardization ==
HKDF was proposed as a building block in various protocols and applications, as well as to discourage the proliferation of multiple KDF mechanisms by its authors.{{r|rfc}}{{rp|1}}

It is formally described in RFC 5869<ref name=rfc>{{cite journal |title=RFC 5869 |last1=Krawczyk |first1=H. |last2=Eronen |first2=P. |url=https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5869 |website=Internet Engineering Task Force |date=May 2010|doi=10.17487/RFC5869 |doi-access=free }}</ref> with detailed analysis in a paper published in 2010.<ref name=iacr>{{cite journal |last=Krawczyk |first=Hugo |title=Cryptographic Extraction and Key Derivation: The HKDF Scheme |journal=Cryptology ePrint Archive |publisher=International Association for Cryptologic Research |date=2010 |url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2010/264}}</ref> NIST SP800-56Cr2<ref>{{cite document|title=NIST Special Publication 800-56C: Recommendation for Key-Derivation Methods in Key-Establishment Schemes |author1=Elaine Barker|author2=Lily Chen|author3=Richard Davis|date=August 2020|doi=10.6028/NIST.SP.800-56Cr2 |doi-access=free |publisher=[[National Institute of Standards and Technology]]}}</ref> specifies a parameterizable extract-then-expand scheme, noting that RFC 5869 HKDF is a version of it and citing its paper for the rationale for the recommendations' extract-and-expand mechanisms.

== Applications ==
HKDF is used in the [[Signal Protocol]] for end-to-end encrypted messaging where it generates the message keys, in conjunction with the triple Elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman handshake (X3DH) key agreement protocol.<ref name="happs">{{cite book |last1=Bhati |first1=Amit Singh |last2=Dufka |first2=Antonín |last3=Andreeva |first3=Elena |last4=Roy |first4=Arnab |last5=Preneel |first5=Bart |title=Proceedings of the 19th ACM Asia Conference on Computer and Communications Security |chapter=Skye: An Expanding PRF based Fast KDF and its Applications |year=2024 |pages=1082–1098 |location=Singapore |isbn=979-8-4007-0482-6 |doi=10.1145/3634737.3637673}}</ref> Signal's "Secure Value Recovery"<ref>{{cite web |url=https://signal.org/blog/secure-value-recovery/ |title=Technology Preview for secure value recovery |last=Lund |first=Joshua |year=2019}}</ref> and "Sealed Sender" are based on HKDF.<ref>{{cite web |title=Technology Preview: Sealed sender for Signal |url=https://signal.org/blog/sealed-sender/ |website=signal.org |last=Lund |first=Joshua |year=2018}}</ref> HKDF is a main component in the [[Noise Protocol Framework]], [[Message Layer Security]], and is used in widely deployed protocols like IPsec [[Internet Key Exchange]] and [[TLS 1.3]].{{r|happs}}

The "multi-purpose" nature of HKDF is meant to serve applications that require key extraction, key expansion, and key hierarchies in [[Key wrap|key wrapping]], [[Key exchange|key exchange]], [[Pseudo random number generator|PRNG]], and [[PBKDF|password-based key derivation]] schemes.<ref>{{cite youtube |title=COST/IACR School on Randomness: Extraction and KDFs I  |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QtlHjixL65M |time=6m |last=Krawczyk |first=Hugo |via=youtube.com |publisher=[[Pompeu Fabra University]] |location=Barcelona |language=en |date= 16 Nov 2016}}</ref>

== Implementations ==

There are implementations of HKDF for [[C Sharp (programming language)|C#]], [[Go (programming language)|Go]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/crypto/hkdf|title=package hkdf |website=pkg.go.dev}}</ref> [[Java (programming language)|Java]], [[JavaScript]], [[Perl]], [[PHP]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.php.net/manual/en/function.hash-hkdf.php|title=hash_hkdf — Generate a HKDF key derivation of a supplied key input |website=php.net}}</ref> [[Python (programming language)|Python]], [[Ruby (programming language)|Ruby]], [[Rust (programming language)|Rust]], and other [[programming language]]s. RFC6234 lays out a reference [[C programming language|C]] implementation of HKDF based on the [[Secure Hash Standard]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6234#section-8.4 |title=US Secure Hash Algorithms (SHA and SHA-based HMAC and HKDF) |last1=Eastlake |first1=Donald |last2=Hansen |first2=Tony |year=2011 |publisher=[[IETF]]}}</ref>

=== Example in Python ===
<syntaxhighlight lang="python3">
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import hashlib
import hmac

# nb: unused here; but SHA512/256 in extract phase provides stronger 
# extraction guarantees when expand is SHA256.
# hash_function_extract = hashlib.sha512
# RFC5869 includes SHA-1 test vectors
hash_function = hashlib.sha256

def hmac_digest(key: bytes, data: bytes) -> bytes:
    return hmac.new(key, data, hash_function).digest()


def hkdf_extract(salt: bytes, ikm: bytes) -> bytes:
    if len(salt) == 0:
        salt = bytes([0] * hash_function().digest_size)
    return hmac_digest(salt, ikm)


def hkdf_expand(prk: bytes, info: bytes, length: int) -> bytes:
    t = b""
    okm = b""
    i = 0
    while len(okm) < length:
        i += 1
        t = hmac_digest(prk, t + info + bytes([i]))
        okm += t
    return okm[:length]


def hkdf(salt: bytes, ikm: bytes, info: bytes, length: int) -> bytes:
    prk = hkdf_extract(salt, ikm)
    return hkdf_expand(prk, info, length)


okm = hkdf(
    salt=bytes.fromhex("000102030405060708090a0b0c"),
    ikm=bytes.fromhex("0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b"),
    info=bytes.fromhex("f0f1f2f3f4f5f6f7f8f9"),
    length=42,
)
assert okm == bytes.fromhex(
    "3cb25f25faacd57a90434f64d0362f2a"
    "2d2d0a90cf1a5a4c5db02d56ecc4c5bf"
    "34007208d5b887185865"
)

# Zero-length salt
assert hkdf(
    salt=b"",
    ikm=bytes.fromhex("0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b"),
    info=b"",
    length=42,
) == bytes.fromhex(
    "8da4e775a563c18f715f802a063c5a31"
    "b8a11f5c5ee1879ec3454e5f3c738d2d"
    "9d201395faa4b61a96c8"
)
</syntaxhighlight>
